title: Naive RAG and Where It Breaks

questions.question: What does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) do?
options: Fine-tunes the model on your documents
Finds relevant text and puts it in the prompt so the model answers from it
questions.explanation: The model's weights don't change; its context does (Phase 4 · Lesson 1).

questions.question: Both refund policies were retrieved, and the answer used the superseded 2024 one. What kind of failure is this?
options: A retrieval failure: the right document was missing
A reading failure: the right text arrived, but the context contradicted itself and the wrong part won
questions.explanation: Retrieval found the current policy; the conflict happened when reading the context.

questions.question: Why did the answer say 'Luis Fe'?
options: Fixed-size chunking cut the name across two chunks, and only the first was retrieved
The name is not in the corpus
questions.explanation: Chunk boundaries decide which facts stay together. Lesson 2 fixes this.

questions.question: Why does the multi-hop question fail even though both needed facts are in the corpus?
options: One retrieval with the original question fetches chunks that look like the question, which only covers the first hop
The model can't do two steps
questions.explanation: The second fact (who is Dana's deputy) only becomes searchable after the first is known.

questions.question: A user asks about a student discount that doesn't exist. Why does naive RAG still answer?
options: Top-k always returns k chunks, and a naive prompt doesn't make 'not in the context' an acceptable answer
Students are in the training data
questions.explanation: Retrieval never returns 'nothing'. Thresholds and self-checking (Lessons 7 and 8) handle this.

questions.question: Your RAG bot gives a wrong answer. What should you check first?
options: The retrieved chunks: was the right text there at all?
questions.explanation: That single check tells you whether to fix retrieval or reading.
